extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and applicants prosecuting US patent applications before the USPTO
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on evaluating and responding to USPTO 'final' Office Actions and Notices of Allowance, and on procedural/strategic choices (responses after final, amendments, RCEs, continuations, appeals, abandonment, and post-allowance amendments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Final Rejection (37 C.F.R. § 1.113)
rubrics_metrics.description: “On the second or any subsequent examination or consideration by the examiner the rejection or other action may be made final, whereupon applicants' reply is limited to appeal in the case of rejection of any claim (§ 1.191), or to amendment as specified in § 1.114 or § 1.116. ... In making such final rejection, the examiner shall repeat or state all grounds of rejection then considered applicable to the claims in the application, clearly stating the reasons in support thereof.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finality limits applicant responses (appeal or limited amendments). Examiner must state and repeat grounds and reasons; applicant replies must comply with §1.114 or §1.116 or appeal. Use this regulatory text to identify when an Office Action is truly final and what reply options remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and proper use of Final Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office introduced the final rejection to conclude prosecution as quickly as possible and discourages switching subject matter in successive amendments or switching between disparate sets of references in successive actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret final rejections as an efficiency tool; applicants should aim to present comprehensive claims and responses in the first Action to avoid unnecessary switching of issues that invite finality. When drafting initial responses, aim to address and avoid all grounds of rejection to limit risk of final rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper bases for issuing a Final Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A final rejection may be proper on a second Office Action (and sometimes on a first Action) where (e.g.) applicant's arguments to prior rejections were unpersuasive, an applicant's amendment necessitated a new search revealing new rejections, or an IDS filed after the first Action raised new grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the examiner had reason to issue finality: repeated, un-overcome grounds; amendments that create need for further search; new prior art submitted in a timely IDS. If these conditions exist, expect finality to be proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a Final Rejection is improper (new ground limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A final rejection is never proper when the examiner introduces a new ground of rejection that is neither (1) necessitated by applicant’s amendment nor (2) based on information submitted in an Information Disclosure Statement filed during the period set forth in 37 C.F.R. 1.97(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a final Action contains a new rejection that does not meet those two predicates, the applicant can argue the final is improper and request withdrawal. Use the MPEP safe-harbor rules to challenge premature final rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe-harbor regarding new art not cited in applicant's IDS
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an originally presented claim is rejected on a new art reference that was not cited in an information disclosure statement by the applicant, a final rejection cannot be properly issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may rely on this safe-harbor when an examiner relies on art not of record (i.e., not cited by applicant in an IDS) to justify a final rejection; argue for withdrawal if relied-upon art was not properly introduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available responses to a Final Action (five paths)
rubrics_metrics.description: To respond to a final Action an applicant may: (1) file a 'response after final' to argue for allowance without amending claims; (2) file an 'amendment and response after final under 37 C.F.R. § 1.116'; (3) re-file as a continuation application under 37 C.F.R. § 1.53; (4) appeal to the Board under 37 C.F.R. § 1.191; or (5) abandon the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider and weigh these mutually exclusive/alternative routes based on the facts: closeness to allowance, desire to avoid narrowing (estoppel), cost/time tradeoffs, and the presence of allowed or objected claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of a Response After Final (no amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A response after final consists of arguing on the merits that the cited references do not apply; e.g., under §102 argue elements not disclosed; under §103 show the examiner failed to set forth a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when the remaining grounds are ministerial or based on minor oversight that, if clarified, will lead to allowance. Restating previously rejected arguments without new substance is unlikely to succeed and wastes resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments and response after final under 37 C.F.R. § 1.116
rubrics_metrics.description: After a final rejection amendments may be made cancelling claims or complying with requirements of form; amendments presenting rejected claims in better form for consideration on appeal may be admitted. Admission or refusal to admit the final amendment will not operate to save the application from abandonment under §1.135.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amend to cancel rejected claims or to obviate the basis of objections/rejections. Substantial claim amendments may be refused entry if they require a new search; such un-entered amendments can be pursued in a continuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: RCE (Request for Continued Examination) rules and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: An RCE removes the finality of the most recent Office Action, allowing additional amendments and consideration; filing an RCE requires a 'submission' that must include a bona fide reply to any outstanding Office Action or it will be improper and not entered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File an RCE when you want to continue prosecution without filing a new continuation; ensure a bona fide reply is included. Note: an RCE does not trigger AIPA patent-term-extension benefits, so consider a continuation instead if patent-term-adjustment is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling claims that are objected-to or allowed in a Final Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Objected-to claims contain allowable subject matter plus formality; rewriting an objected claim in independent format (inserting limitations and removing dependency) will generally overcome the objection; if allowed claims are of sufficient breadth applicant may pay issue fees to obtain an earlier patent, or pursue rejected claims in a continuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to take immediate allowance (cost/benefit: issue and maintenance fees, presence of infringers, breadth of coverage) or to continue prosecution for broader protection. Cancel rejected claims without prejudice and pursue them in a continuation if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation practice and priority/ publication constraints (37 C.F.R. § 1.53(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: For continuations filed under §1.53(b) any priority claim back to the parent must be made by the later of 16 months from the filing of the parent application or 4 months from the filing of the continuation; continuation applications filed under §1.53(b) will be published unless applicant files a request for non-publication at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pursuing cancelled claims in continuations, observe the strict priority-claim timing and place of publication/non-publication choices; consider including preliminary remarks in the new application to expedite prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal eligibility and timing (35 U.S.C. §134 / 37 C.F.R. §1.191)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may appeal any claim in a pending application that has been twice rejected. The applicant must file a timely Notice of Appeal within three months (extensions up to six months with fees are available) and pay the separate appeal fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal is an option when prosecution has stalled and narrowing is undesirable; weigh the time and expense against RCE/continuation strategies. Ensure the timeliness of Notice of Appeal and payment of required fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal Brief formal content and argument requirements (37 C.F.R. §1.192)
rubrics_metrics.description: An Appeal Brief must include specified items in order (real party in interest; related appeals; status of claims; status of amendments; summary of invention; issues; grouping of claims; argument; appendix). In 'grouping of claims' appellant must group claims that stand or fall together; in 'argument' appellant must provide factual and legal bases with citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strictly follow formal requirements; group claims thoughtfully to allow a representative claim to be decided; provide legal authority and specific arguments (do not rely solely on familiar prosecution-style arguments). Noncompliance may lead to rejection of the brief and dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal conference and Examiner’s Answer limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: After an Appeal Brief is filed the examiner must hold an appeal conference or withdraw the rejection; the appeal conference (examiner, SPE, third examiner) can lead to withdrawal. If they maintain the rejection, an Examiner's Answer is issued, which may not include a new ground of rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare the Appeal Brief to anticipate examiner positions and to encourage withdrawal at the appeal conference. Because Examiner's Answers cannot add new rejections, strategic briefing can foreclose examiner positions or force reopening prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reply Brief and oral hearing timing and use
rubrics_metrics.description: After the Examiner's Answer, the applicant has two months to file a Reply Brief (optional) and two months to request an oral hearing (fee required); hearings should be requested only when necessary, e.g., complex technological issues better argued orally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Reply Brief to focus and rebut the Examiner's Answer. Request oral hearing selectively for complex technical disputes where two-way communication will be beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board decision outcomes and post-decision options
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may affirm, reverse, remand, or take other actions. If reversed, the case is forwarded to the examiner for action and the examiner is discouraged from doing a new search; if affirmed, applicant may abandon, continue prosecution via continuation, petition for rehearing, seek a civil action under 35 U.S.C. §145, or appeal to the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate possible outcomes and plan next steps (e.g., obtain narrower immediate protection while pursuing broader claims by continuation and appeal). Consider timing and cost of further appeals or civil actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment as a deliberate option
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may explicitly abandon the application under 37 C.F.R. § 1.138 or allow it to lapse by failing to reply within statutory periods (three-month shortened period plus three-month extension up to six months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use abandonment when the invention is not worth further prosecution (e.g., unpatentable over cited references, narrow little-value claims, or cost reasons). Be mindful of deadlines to avoid inadvertent abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time periods for Responding to a Final Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically a shortened statutory period of response expires three months from mailing of the final Action. If reply is filed within two months, the shortened statutory period will expire three months from the date of the final Action or on the date the advisory action is mailed, whichever is later. Responses filed after two months may be filed but must not exceed the six-month statutory limit (or the application will be abandoned).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track two- and three-month markers carefully. If not responsive within two months, ensure any later reply still places the application 'in condition for allowance' before the six-month cutoff, or pursue RCE/continuation/appeal as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy considerations in choosing a post-final course
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether examiner understands the invention and cited references (consider interview), whether narrowing will be acceptable, whether an RCE is cost-effective if close to agreement, and whether an appeal is appropriate after all reasonable amendments are exhausted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interviews to clear misunderstandings; prefer RCE when close to agreement; pursue appeal only after exhausting reasonable amendments and considering cost/time tradeoffs; consider continuation to obtain some protection quickly while pursuing broader claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques to avoid a Final Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Advanced planning can help avoid final rejections: include independent claims of varying scope (broad and narrow) at filing, conduct prior art searches pre-filing, and when submitting newly identified prior art in an IDS consider amending pending claims to avoid anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft initial claim sets with fallback scopes and perform good pre-filing searches. Use timely IDS and claim drafting to minimize likelihood of a second-action final rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner reasons for allowance and cautions (post-allowance statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the record does not make clear the reasons for allowing a claim, the examiner should provide specific reasons for allowance; each statement should include at least (1) the major difference in the claims not found in the prior art of record, and (2) why the claim is considered patentable over the prior art if not clear in the record. Care must be taken to ensure statements are accurate and not unduly broad or narrow due to possible estoppel effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully review any examiner reasons for allowance because statements become part of file history and may create estoppel; if disagree, submit remarks before or with payment of the issue fee to clarify the prosecution record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant remarks in response to Examiner reasons for allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant should carefully review examiner reasons for allowance and may provide comments to be included in the file history if she disagrees, preferably before or with payment of the issue fee. An examiner may not respond; silence does not mean agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File clarifying remarks promptly (before paying issue fee) to preserve distinctions and avoid negative inferences. Do not assume examiner concurrence from lack of reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments after Notice of Allowance (37 C.F.R. § 1.312) — limits and entry criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: No amendment may be made as a matter of right after mailing of a Notice of Allowance. Any amendment must be filed before or with payment of the issue fee and may be entered on recommendation of the primary examiner and approval by the Commissioner. Examiners may enter only formal corrections or formal claim matter changes that do not change claim scope; substantive amendments require justification and may be refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid needing post-allowance amendments by being diligent earlier in prosecution. If substantive change is necessary before issue, include required remarks explaining why the amendment is needed and why no additional search or examination is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required showing for substantive post-allowance amendments (MPEP § 716.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: For substantive amendments after allowance applicant must fully and clearly state reasons showing (1) why the amendment is needed; (2) why the proposed amended or new claims require no additional search or examination; (3) why the claims are patentable; and (4) why they were not presented earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide comprehensive remarks addressing each required element. Failure to do so may result in refusal to enter the amendment. Ensure amendments do not materially change disclosure or require substantial PTO work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of examiner statements in file history and estoppel risk
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner’s statement regarding allowability is significant for the file history and may have estoppel effects (e.g., Zenith Labs Inc. v. Bristol-Myers Squibb Co.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat any reasons for allowance as potentially binding part of the prosecution history. Craft applicant remarks and amendments carefully to avoid creating disadvantageous admissions or limiting constructions.
